newsitem.title: USA: US oil union seeks legal options after takeovers.
newsitem.headline: US oil union seeks legal options after takeovers.

text.p: With a wave of mergers in the U.S. oil refining sector in the past year or so, the main union representing workers in the industry is developing a new legal strategy to fend off what it sees as attacks on its members' rights.

No fewer than 11 major companies have either concluded mergers or announced plans to consolidate their refining operations in the past 12 to 18 months. Members of the Oil Chemical and Atomic Workers union (OCAW), in some cases, have seen new owners throw out agreements signed with the old company.

The acquiring companies are able to do this legally because courts have interpreted in their favor a 1972 Supreme Court ruling (Burns Security Services vs National Labor Relations Board), effectively releasing them from labor agreements reached with the previous owners, according to Larry Cary, partner and labor attorney with Vladeck, Waldman, Elias and Englehard in New York..
Tosco Corp, for example, was successful in forcing new agreements when it took over BP Oil and Unocal Corp plants.
Citgo Petroleum Corp, ultimately owned by state Petroleos de Venezuela, is in the process of trying to get a new agreement at a Lemont, Illinois plant which it recently began operating.
Some other acquiring companies, while not saying outright that they plan to seek new labor agreements, are keeping their options opened.
And unions are worried.
The new tack which the union is developing will focus on the interpretation of the old company's intention of what should happen in the event the company was taken over.
"Sometimes an issue arises if there is a 'successor clause' in the contracts," said Greg Mooney, general counsel for the Oil, Chemical and Atomic Workers union (OCAW).

There are different kinds of 'successor clauses' but basically they address what happens when a new owner takes over. So far, existing contracts must have language that explicitly bars the sale of the company unless the new owner agrees to honor the labor contract.

However, OCAW is going to try to persuade the court to recognize that the inclusion of any successor clause implies that the intention of the seller was for the new owner to recognize the existing labor contract.
"We may get to test our view of that successor clause," said Mooney. "Next time out of the box we'll seek to enjoin the transaction," he added.
The Citgo case is the only current dispute which touches on Burns, but this may not be an ideal one to test the union's new strategy.

Citgo's contends that it is a new company and that it was not a party to the agreement reached last year with the previous owner UNO-VEN. But the union has a strong argument that, whether or not the existing agreement has explicit 'successor clause' language about a takeover, Citgo is a successor company as its parent was a 50 percent owner of UNO-VEN when it signed the agreement.
Rather, the real fight over the issue may be with one of the other companies involved in the spate of takeovers.

Shell and Texaco, which are about half-way through completing the largest downstream deal in the history of the industry, have said the current labor agreements will be honored if the Federal Trade Commission clears their merger.
USX Corp's Marathon, which is set to become a 62 percent owner of a refining merger with Ashland was less clear about what would happen to its union agreeements.
""Right now we're not prepared to discuss that. It's way to early... we'll work at the pieces later on," said Bill Ryder, company spokesman.
Ultramar Diamond Shamrock also was unwilling to address the issue until their bid to buy to Total is finalized in a couple of months.
